items.stem: Which of the following best describes "speech bubble"?
options: A sequence of sketches or descriptions planning each shot or panel
A shape containing a character's spoken words, with a tail pointing to the speaker
What is included in a panel and how it is arranged, including tilted (Dutch) frames
A new version of a text in a different form or medium, such as a story turned into a comic or film
items.answer: A shape containing a character's spoken words, with a tail pointing to the speaker
items.markingKey: B. "speech bubble" is a shape containing a character's spoken words, with a tail pointing to the speaker.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a silent panel can be powerful.
items.answer: Without words, the reader slows down and focuses on expression and image, often showing strong emotion.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Without words, the reader slows down and focuses on expression and image, often showing strong emotion. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Graphic novels are just picture books for younger readers." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Graphic novels tell complex stories for all ages, combining images and words in sophisticated ways.
items.markingKey: Graphic novels tell complex stories for all ages, combining images and words in sophisticated ways. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Describe two panels showing a character receiving bad news: state the shot and what the speech bubble or caption says.
items.answer: Any two coherent panels, e.g. Panel 1 medium shot of a girl reading a phone, caption "Then the message came."; Panel 2 close-up of her face, no words. Credit purposeful choices.
items.markingKey: Any two coherent panels, e.g. Panel 1 medium shot of a girl reading a phone, caption "Then the message came."; Panel 2 close-up of her face, no words. Credit purposeful choices.

items.stem:
Read the following graphic novel page described in words.

PANEL 1 (wide, from above): Two tiny figures on a rooftop at sunset; the whole city spreads beneath them. Caption: "The last night before Kofi moved away."
PANEL 2 (medium shot): Kofi and Ama sit side by side, legs dangling. No words.
PANEL 3 (close-up): Ama's hand holds out a paper aeroplane. Speech bubble: "Promise you'll write."
PANEL 4 (extreme close-up, all colour drained to grey): Kofi's eyes, wet. Tiny speech bubble: "Every day."

Explain the effect of the symbolic object in this page.
items.answer: Symbolic object: "a paper aeroplane" – the aeroplane symbolises the distance and the letters that will keep the friendship alive.
items.markingKey: Symbolic object: "a paper aeroplane" – the aeroplane symbolises the distance and the letters that will keep the friendship alive. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Graphic novels require less reading skill than prose novels."
items.answer: Graphic novels demand different skills – visual and verbal reading at once – rather than fewer skills.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: images give information quickly; less text. Arguments against: readers must interpret images, panels, gutters and text together; visual literacy is complex. Supported judgement: Graphic novels demand different skills – visual and verbal reading at once – rather than fewer skills.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A single frame or box in a comic or graphic novel showing one moment"?
items.answer: panel
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of panel.

items.stem: Distinguish between a speech bubble and a caption.
items.answer: A speech bubble contains a character's spoken words and points to the speaker; a caption is a box, usually narration or context, not spoken aloud by a character in the scene.
items.markingKey: A speech bubble contains a character's spoken words and points to the speaker; a caption is a box, usually narration or context, not spoken aloud by a character in the scene. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the following graphic novel page described in words.

PANEL 1 (low angle): A double-decker bus looms out of thick fog, headlights glaring. Sound effect in jagged letters: "SKREEEE!"
PANEL 2 (medium shot): Nia, 13, steps aboard. The bus is empty. Caption: "The 11:45. The last bus. Or so I thought."
PANEL 3 (over-the-shoulder shot): The driver's reflection in the mirror – he has no face.
PANEL 4 (wide, tilted frame): The bus speeds away. Every window now has a passenger staring out.

Analyse the effect of the silent or wordless moments on this page.
items.answer: The four panels build a horror sequence: arrival, entering, discovery and a final shock. The gutters between panels force the reader to imagine what happens in between (when did the passengers appear?), which adds to the fear.
items.markingKey: The four panels build a horror sequence: arrival, entering, discovery and a final shock. The gutters between panels force the reader to imagine what happens in between (when did the passengers appear?), which adds to the fear. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Define the term "camera angle".
items.answer: The position from which a subject is viewed: high angle (looking down), low angle (looking up), eye level
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the position from which a subject is viewed: high angle (looking down), low angle (looking up), eye level. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a low-angle shot and a high-angle shot.
items.answer: A high-angle shot looks down on a subject, making it seem small or vulnerable; a low-angle shot looks up, making it seem powerful or threatening.
items.markingKey: A high-angle shot looks down on a subject, making it seem small or vulnerable; a low-angle shot looks up, making it seem powerful or threatening. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Mohammed writes: "Colour in a graphic novel is just decoration." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Colour creates mood and meaning, such as warm sunset tones for nostalgia or grey for sadness.
items.markingKey: Colour creates mood and meaning, such as warm sunset tones for nostalgia or grey for sadness. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Describe the colour palette you would use for a panel showing a happy memory, and why.
items.answer: E.g. warm golden tones and soft edges to suggest warmth and nostalgia.
items.markingKey: E.g. warm golden tones and soft edges to suggest warmth and nostalgia.

Explain how the visual choices on this page help to present the theme of the supernatural and fear.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "In graphic novels, images matter more than words."
items.answer: Images often carry the most information, but the strongest pages combine images and words so that each adds something the other cannot.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: images carry setting, emotion and action; silent panels show power of images. Arguments against: words give voice, narration and humour; meaning comes from the interplay. Supported judgement: Images often carry the most information, but the strongest pages combine images and words so that each adds something the other cannot.

items.stem: What is the usual effect of a low-angle shot?
options: It makes the subject look small and weak
It makes the subject look powerful or threatening
items.answer: It makes the subject look powerful or threatening
items.markingKey: B. Looking up makes things loom.

items.stem: Briefly explain why artists vary shot distance across a page.
items.answer: Moving from wide to close shots controls focus and emotion – wide shots set the scene, close-ups intensify feeling.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Moving from wide to close shots controls focus and emotion – wide shots set the scene, close-ups intensify feeling. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: What is the first step in adapting a scene into a comic strip?
options: Identifying the key moments to show in each panel
Writing the title in bubble letters
items.answer: Identifying the key moments to show in each panel
items.markingKey: B. Planning the sequence comes first.

items.stem: Explain why adapting a story into a comic requires cutting words.
items.answer: Images show setting, action and emotion, so description and some dialogue become unnecessary; captions are kept short.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Images show setting, action and emotion, so description and some dialogue become unnecessary; captions are kept short. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain which part of the attic extract you would show as a silent panel, and why.
items.answer: E.g. the close-up of Leila's hand on the warm handle, with no words, to slow the pace and build suspense.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a novel about starting a new school.

Mei stood at the classroom door clutching a timetable she had folded so many times it was soft as cloth.
Twenty-eight faces turned. Someone laughed – not at her, probably, but her cheeks burned anyway.
"There's a seat here," said a girl with silver braces and paint on her fingers. She shoved a pile of comics aside. "I'm Zara. Do you like drawing? Please say yes. Nobody here likes drawing."
Mei, who had filled three sketchbooks on the plane from Shanghai, almost smiled.
"Yes," she said. It was the first word she had spoken all day.

Adapt this extract into a short comic: describe three panels, explaining how each shot creates the mood of the original.
items.answer: A nervous girl, Mei, arrives at a new school from Shanghai; a friendly classmate, Zara, invites her to sit down and asks if she likes drawing, and Mei speaks her first word of the day.
items.markingKey: A nervous girl, Mei, arrives at a new school from Shanghai; a friendly classmate, Zara, invites her to sit down and asks if she likes drawing, and Mei speaks her first word of the day. Mark mainly against criterion C (Producing text) and D (Using language), with B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: imaginative, insightful response with deliberate stylistic choices for effect, a controlled structure and varied, precise, accurate language; 5-6: substantial engagement and mostly effective choices; 3-4: adequate but uneven; 1-2: limited, with frequent errors that obscure meaning.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "A comic-strip adaptation is always simpler than the original story."
items.answer: Adaptations are different rather than simpler; they lose some narration but gain visual meaning.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: text is cut; inner thoughts are harder to show. Arguments against: images add new layers of meaning; panel layout and colour create complexity. Supported judgement: Adaptations are different rather than simpler; they lose some narration but gain visual meaning.

items.stem: Explain why sound effects are useful when adapting a suspense story into a comic.
items.answer: Written sounds (a creak, a knock) can be shown as lettering inside the image, recreating the tension that narration created in the story.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Written sounds (a creak, a knock) can be shown as lettering inside the image, recreating the tension that narration created in the story. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between narration in a story and captions in a comic.
items.answer: A story's narrator can describe at length; a comic's captions must be brief, because images carry most of the description.
items.markingKey: A story's narrator can describe at length; a comic's captions must be brief, because images carry most of the description. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.answer: Readers imagine the action between panels (closure), which involves them actively and can create suspense or humour.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a novel about a boy who eats lunch alone.

Every lunchtime Oliver ate on the bench behind the music block, where the wind smelled of old leaves and nobody came.
He told his mum he had loads of friends. It was easier than the truth.
On Tuesday, a tuba case appeared at the other end of the bench, followed by a tall girl with a sandwich.
"Is this your bench?" she asked.
"It's nobody's bench," Oliver said.
"Good," said the girl, sitting down. "Then it can be ours."

Plan a four-panel comic strip adaptation of this extract. For each panel, describe the shot and write one caption or speech bubble.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "camera angle"?
options: A box of text, often narration, giving context, time or a narrator's thoughts
The position from which a subject is viewed: high angle (looking down), low angle (looking up), eye level
A sequence of sketches or descriptions planning each shot or panel
A small, rough sketch used to plan the layout of panels
items.answer: The position from which a subject is viewed: high angle (looking down), low angle (looking up), eye level
items.markingKey: B. "camera angle" is the position from which a subject is viewed: high angle (looking down), low angle (looking up), eye level.

items.stem: A student claims: "Every sentence of the story needs its own panel." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Adapters choose key moments; some sentences become one panel, others are cut, and some moments are stretched across several panels for pacing.
items.markingKey: Adapters choose key moments; some sentences become one panel, others are cut, and some moments are stretched across several panels for pacing. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a caption and a speech bubble.
items.answer: A speech bubble contains a character's spoken words and points to the speaker; a caption is a box, usually narration or context, not spoken aloud by a character in the scene.
items.markingKey: A speech bubble contains a character's spoken words and points to the speaker; a caption is a box, usually narration or context, not spoken aloud by a character in the scene. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between a low-angle shot and a high-angle shot.
items.answer: A high-angle shot looks down on a subject, making it seem small or vulnerable; a low-angle shot looks up, making it seem powerful or threatening.
items.markingKey: A high-angle shot looks down on a subject, making it seem small or vulnerable; a low-angle shot looks up, making it seem powerful or threatening. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Diego writes: "A character's thoughts cannot be shown in a comic." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Thoughts can be shown through thought bubbles, captions, facial expressions in close-up, or symbolic images.
items.markingKey: Thoughts can be shown through thought bubbles, captions, facial expressions in close-up, or symbolic images. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following graphic novel page described in words.

PANEL 1 (low angle): A double-decker bus looms out of thick fog, headlights glaring. Sound effect in jagged letters: "SKREEEE!"
PANEL 2 (medium shot): Nia, 13, steps aboard. The bus is empty. Caption: "The 11:45. The last bus. Or so I thought."
PANEL 3 (over-the-shoulder shot): The driver's reflection in the mirror – he has no face.
PANEL 4 (wide, tilted frame): The bus speeds away. Every window now has a passenger staring out.

Why might the creator have used a caption with foreshadowing here?
items.answer: Caption with foreshadowing: ""The last bus. Or so I thought."" – Nia's retrospective narration hints that something strange is coming.
items.markingKey: Caption with foreshadowing: ""The last bus. Or so I thought."" – Nia's retrospective narration hints that something strange is coming. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Choose a shot distance and angle for a panel showing a hero facing a giant robot, and explain your choice.
items.answer: E.g. a low-angle wide shot from behind the hero, making the robot loom and the hero look brave but small. Credit choice + reason.
items.markingKey: E.g. a low-angle wide shot from behind the hero, making the robot loom and the hero look brave but small. Credit choice + reason.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a short story set in a tower block in Hong Kong.

The lift stopped between the 23rd and 24th floors with a soft clunk.
The lights dimmed to emergency orange. Kenji pressed the alarm. Nothing.
'Don't worry,' said the old woman in the corner. 'It happens every Tuesday.'
It was Wednesday.
Kenji looked at her properly for the first time. Her umbrella was dripping, though it hadn't rained all week. And in the mirrored wall, where her reflection should have been, there was only an umbrella, dripping, all by itself.

Adapt this extract into a short comic: describe three panels, explaining how each shot creates the mood of the original.
items.answer: Kenji is trapped in a stuck lift with an old woman who says it happens every Tuesday – but it is Wednesday, her umbrella is wet in a dry week, and she has no reflection.
items.markingKey: Kenji is trapped in a stuck lift with an old woman who says it happens every Tuesday – but it is Wednesday, her umbrella is wet in a dry week, and she has no reflection. Mark mainly against criterion C (Producing text) and D (Using language), with B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: imaginative, insightful response with deliberate stylistic choices for effect, a controlled structure and varied, precise, accurate language; 5-6: substantial engagement and mostly effective choices; 3-4: adequate but uneven; 1-2: limited, with frequent errors that obscure meaning.

items.stem:
Read the following graphic novel page described in words.

PANEL 1 (wide, from above): Two tiny figures on a rooftop at sunset; the whole city spreads beneath them. Caption: "The last night before Kofi moved away."
PANEL 2 (medium shot): Kofi and Ama sit side by side, legs dangling. No words.
PANEL 3 (close-up): Ama's hand holds out a paper aeroplane. Speech bubble: "Promise you'll write."
PANEL 4 (extreme close-up, all colour drained to grey): Kofi's eyes, wet. Tiny speech bubble: "Every day."

How does the writer use panels, captions and gutters to control the reader's experience?
items.answer: The page moves from a wide, distant establishing shot to an extreme close-up, drawing the reader closer to the characters' emotions. The silent second panel uses the gutter and lack of words to show a pause full of feeling, and the caption gives context the images cannot.
items.markingKey: The page moves from a wide, distant establishing shot to an extreme close-up, drawing the reader closer to the characters' emotions. The silent second panel uses the gutter and lack of words to show a pause full of feeling, and the caption gives context the images cannot. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Describe the shot distance and angle you would use to show (a) a character feeling lonely in a big city and (b) a bully looming over a victim, explaining each.
items.answer: (a) a wide, high-angle shot making the character tiny against buildings; (b) a low-angle shot from the victim's viewpoint so the bully looms. 1 mark each choice, 1 each reason.
items.markingKey: (a) a wide, high-angle shot making the character tiny against buildings; (b) a low-angle shot from the victim's viewpoint so the bully looms. 1 mark each choice, 1 each reason.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a suspense story.

The attic door had been locked for as long as Leila could remember. 'Nothing up there but dust,' Gran always said.
So why, tonight, was there a light under it?
Leila climbed the stairs. Each step creaked. Each creak sounded like a warning.
She reached for the handle. It was warm.
Behind the door, something was humming – a tune she knew. The tune her mother used to sing.
Her mother had been gone for six years.

Plan a four-panel comic strip adaptation of this extract. For each panel, describe the shot and write one caption or speech bubble.
items.answer: Leila sees a light under the locked attic door, climbs the creaking stairs and hears someone humming her mother's tune – but her mother has been gone for six years.
items.markingKey: Leila sees a light under the locked attic door, climbs the creaking stairs and hears someone humming her mother's tune – but her mother has been gone for six years. Mark mainly against criterion C (Producing text) and D (Using language), with B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: imaginative, insightful response with deliberate stylistic choices for effect, a controlled structure and varied, precise, accurate language; 5-6: substantial engagement and mostly effective choices; 3-4: adequate but uneven; 1-2: limited, with frequent errors that obscure meaning.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Graphic novels require less reading skill than prose novels."
items.answer: Graphic novels demand different skills – visual and verbal reading at once – rather than fewer skills.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: images give information quickly; less text. Arguments against: readers must interpret images, panels, gutters and text together; visual literacy is complex. Supported judgement: Graphic novels demand different skills – visual and verbal reading at once – rather than fewer skills.

items.stem: "In graphic novels, images matter more than words." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Images often carry the most information, but the strongest pages combine images and words so that each adds something the other cannot.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: images carry setting, emotion and action; silent panels show power of images. Arguments against: words give voice, narration and humour; meaning comes from the interplay. Supported judgement: Images often carry the most information, but the strongest pages combine images and words so that each adds something the other cannot. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criteria (each 0-8, scaled to this item). A Analysing: explains content, context, language, structure, technique and style and their effects; justifies opinions with examples and explanation, using terminology. B Organising: a clear, logical structure suited to the task; ideas linked with purpose; referencing conventions. C Producing text: insight, imagination and personal engagement; deliberate stylistic choices; relevant detail and examples. D Using language: varied, accurate vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression; appropriate register and style; accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. 7-8 perceptive/excellent; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: "A comic-strip adaptation is always simpler than the original story." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Adaptations are different rather than simpler; they lose some narration but gain visual meaning.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: text is cut; inner thoughts are harder to show. Arguments against: images add new layers of meaning; panel layout and colour create complexity.
